Issued at 315 PM CDT Mon Sep 14 2026

Rest of Today - Tonight:

An increasingly vertically-stacked low pressure system currently
over the Dakotas will slide northeast into southern Manitoba
this evening and far northwest Ontario tonight into early 
Tuesday. An attendant surface occluded front with this system
will also move west to east across the Northland this evening
and tonight. An area of strong isentropic lift ahead of the
front has led to widespread rain showers with a few embedded, 
non-severe thunderstorms spreading southwest to northeast 
across the Northland, arriving latest in northwest Wisconsin 
mid-afternoon. Expect this area of rain to continue through 
this evening into early tonight, ending from west to east as the
occluded front moves through. The isolated, embedded 
thunderstorm potential persists through early/mid evening
(generally ending around 8-10 PM) as elevated instability 
of 100-400 J/kg MUCAPE will be present. Despite strong bulk
shear, this limited instability combined with marginal lapse 
rates aloft (6 degC/km or less) should keep most thunderstorms
that do develop as general in nature. Can't rule out a strong
storm or two late this afternoon through early/mid-evening,
mainly in northwest Wisconsin, with hail of one-half inch or
smaller and heavy downpours leading to ponding of water on roads
and low-lying areas as the main threats. Gusty southeast 
synoptic winds continue to increase through the rest of this
afternoon into evening ahead of the front, with gusts up to
around 35 mph. We will see a brief lull in winds behind the
front later this evening into early tonight before winds
increase out of the west again by late tonight/early 
Tuesday morning.

Regarding precipitation, additional rainfall amounts of 0.5" to
around 1" are forecast for the remainder of this afternoon into
tonight. Highest amounts remain from central Minnesota into the
Iron Range and across far inland northwest Wisconsin. While
periodic higher rain rates are possible with any thunderstorms,
the more showery nature of these storms should preclude flash
flooding, with some patchy ponding on roadways and in low-lying
areas being the main concern. This is a welcome rainfall given 
ongoing drought conditions.

Tuesday - Tuesday Night:

Even stronger winds with gusts of 30 to  strong west to 
northwest winds with gusts up to 30 to 40 mph develop on Tuesday
out of the west as the surface pressure gradient remains tight
with the low pressure system moving across northwestern Ontario.
Wrap around cold air advection and lingering, shallow moisture
should keep cloud cover going across much of the Northland
Tuesday morning and in far north-central/northern Minnesota
through the afternoon and evening. We have also introduced some
sprinkle/slight chance (10-20%) rain shower mention in far
northern Minnesota on Tuesday, as well. As the low departs
farther to the northeast later in the day, winds and gusts will
be on a decreasing trend. Slightly below normal high
temperatures in the low 60s to around 70F are forecast, warmest
in northwest Wisconsin. Light winds, clearing skies, and high
pressure settling in on Tuesday night will allow low
temperatures to drop into the upper 30s to low 40s, being
slightly warmer near Lake Superior and slightly colder into the
mid 30s for typical cold spots. Patchy frost is possible in the
typical cold spots where temperatures fall into the mid 30s, but
widespread frost is unlikely (less than 30% chance of
occurrence).

Wednesday - Thursday:

A zonal flow pattern aloft sets up for Wednesday and Thursday.
Wednesday will be dry to start, but there is potential for some
light rain showers (10-40%) across far northern and southern
portions of the Northland Wednesday evening into early Wednesday
night as the high pressure departs to the east. An additional 
surface high pressure center passing to our north Thursday
should keep that day dry.

Temperatures moderate slightly for Wednesday and Thursday with
high temperatures in the mid 60s to low 70s on
Wednesday/Thursday, and some mid 70s in the Brainerd Lakes to
northwest Wisconsin on Thursday. Relatively warmer lows in the
40s to low 50s (warmest near Lake Superior) Wednesday and
Thursday nights should keep any additional frost chances at bay.

Friday - This Coming Weekend:

Another round of showers and thunderstorms are forecast to
return to the Northland on Friday through early Saturday. Lee 
cyclogenesis develops a surface low in eastern Colorado on
Thursday and ejects it through the Central Plains Thursday
night/early Friday and into the Upper Mississippi River Valley
late Friday into early Saturday. The exact track of the surface
low and the northward extent of its attendant warm front and
warm sector will dictate precipitation potential, amounts, and
locations in the Northland for Friday through early Saturday.
